strengths: Well-motivated practical problem domain (500M Excel users) with clear societal relevance and understudied status

Comprehensive, multi-layered evaluation framework integrating programmatic features (29 well-defined metrics), data-driven failure taxonomy (validated 78% with experts), and domain-expert evaluation—providing valuable triangulation
Methodologically rigorous: proper application of Bradley-Terry model with feature augmentation, appropriate causal disclaimers, thorough feature significance testing across domains
Important empirical finding that crowd preferences diverge from professional financial standards (42.3% expert-crowd agreement), with clear implications for RLHF-based post-training
Exceptional reproducibility: comprehensive appendices with system prompts, JSON schema, 29 feature definitions, model configs, failure taxonomy, evaluation rubrics; promised dataset release
Novel combination of techniques in new domain: Arena evaluation + feature decomposition + failure taxonomy applied to end-to-end spreadsheet generation at scale (4,357 votes, 16 models)

Multi-domain insights: Dramatic domain-specific ranking shifts (Claude 1st→9th in Academic domain) reveal that evaluation criteria fundamentally vary by use case, supporting use-case-dependent preference modeling
Live platform and dataset provide lasting community value beyond the paper's immediate findings
weaknesses: Expert-crowd disagreement (42.3% overall, 56.4% for decisive cases) is documented but not deeply explained—paper fails to analyze why professionals and crowds value different attributes, limiting insights for future work

Low inter-rater reliability in expert study (Krippendorff's α: 0.27–0.51) undermines confidence in the expert ground truth and raises questions about whether 'professional standards' are contested even among domain experts

Concerning feature effects: Formula sophistication (lookups, conditionals, constants) shows no significant association with preferences while presentation features (text density +1.56, fills +1.15) dominate—suggests preference signals reward style over substance, but paper doesn't explore why or propose mitigation

Limited actionability: Paper provides rankings and feature analysis but minimal guidance on how to improve spreadsheet generation; vague references to 'upstream interventions' and 'data curation' without concrete proposals
Task formulation constraints: Assumes single end-to-end JSON generation, excluding iterative/agentic approaches that professionals commonly use; limits generalizability of findings

Failure taxonomy validation uses circular pipeline (GPT-5-mini generates rationales → cluster → hand-curate → validate on 50 samples), risking bias toward LLM-derived failure categories; no independent expert categorization

Insufficient analysis of dramatic domain-specific reversals (e.g., Academic & Research rankings completely shuffle); explanation of number formatting coefficient (-5.38) is plausible but under-explored
Low inter-rater agreement in expert study combined with small sample (15 triply-rated, 89 single-rated) limits confidence in reliability dimension of expert evaluation

Missing important experimental details: Arena URL blank in paper; prompt complexity distribution not provided; vote distribution per prompt/model pair unclear; no analysis of systematic model disagreements
Primarily a dataset/evaluation paper with limited algorithmic innovation; doesn't advance spreadsheet generation methods themselves, only characterizes what exists

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task domain: spreadsheet generation is genuinely understudied relative to its 500M user base; spreadsheets have greater structural complexity than code or JSON
Comprehensive multi-layered evaluation approach: arena voting, feature decomposition, data-driven failure taxonomy, and expert evaluation provide complementary perspectives

Empirically substantive findings: domain-specific feature effects (sign reversals across domains), distinctive model failure profiles, and the insight that formatting outweighs formula complexity in crowd preferences
Rigorous validation attempts: 78% agreement between LLM judge and 50 expert samples for failure taxonomy; systematic expert evaluation study with defined rubrics across 6 dimensions
Valuable dataset contribution: promise to release 4,357 preference votes with prompts, spreadsheets, and failure categorizations could enable future research
weaknesses: Fundamental validity crisis inadequately addressed: crowd preferences agree with expert judgment only 42.3% overall (56.4% among decisive comparisons—barely better than chance). This critically undermines the core premise that blind preference voting is a valid evaluation signal, yet the paper treats this as a minor observation rather than engaging substantively with its implications

Limited methodological novelty: Bradley-Terry + Elo, feature-augmented models, arena-style evaluation, and LLM-as-judge are all straightforward applications of established techniques (Coulom 2007, Scale AI 2025, Chiang et al. 2024, Deng et al. 2025). No novel ranking algorithm, evaluation theory, or principled approach to crowd-expert disagreement

Artificial task formulation with questionable generalizability: single end-to-end JSON generation without iteration, user feedback, or refinement cycles is unrealistic for actual spreadsheet workflows. Authors acknowledge alternative 'iterative or agentic' approaches but don't explore them

Feature analysis shows signs of measuring domain artifacts rather than true quality: pct_number_format reverses sign dramatically across domains (Academic: −5.38, Finance: +0.61), suggesting features capture annotation artifacts. Massive Elo compression after feature adjustment (Claude Opus −217 points) indicates model rankings are largely stylistic variation. Only 16/29 features significant globally

Questionable central claims: (1) 'Challenging task'—Claude Opus wins 83.5% of battles, suggesting limited challenge; (2) 'Substantial domain variation'—only Academic and Finance deeply analyzed (2 domains insufficient); (3) 'Models lack best practices'—based on 52 battles with low inter-rater reliability (α = 0.27–0.51)

Small, underpowered expert study: 52 battles yielding 104 spreadsheets and 134 evaluations; only 5 evaluators from single background (investment banking); low inter-rater reliability (α = 0.27–0.51) indicates unclear or disagreeable rubric dimensions; finance is ~1–2% of arena battles

Data quality and potential biases: 4,357 votes distributed unevenly across 436 seed prompts plus unknown user submissions; invalid outputs discarded and replaced (potential differential invalidity bias); model configurations vary dramatically (temperature, token limits differ); 8.5% 'both are bad' votes handling unclear; K-NN classification of user prompts has unreported error rate

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals on Elo ratings, no multiple comparison correction across domains, no justification for Bradley-Terry transitivity assumption, small subgroup sample sizes (e.g., Finance rankings based on ~52 battles)

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied domain: spreadsheet generation for 500M Excel users, establishing the first comprehensive arena-style benchmark

Comprehensive multi-perspective evaluation framework combining three complementary methodologies: programmatic features (29 features across 4 categories), data-driven failure taxonomy (7 categories, 78% agreement with human annotators), and expert rubric grounded in professional finance conventions

Clear, honest presentation of uncomfortable findings: formula sophistication features show no significance; expert-crowd agreement is only 56.4% (barely above chance); formatting drives preferences more than correctness

Well-executed empirical analysis with rigorous methodology: Bradley-Terry modeling with feature augmentation properly qualified, domain-specific analysis revealing Academic/Finance preference reversals, appropriate caveats on causality vs. regression adjustment

Strong reproducibility and community value: live arena platform, promise to release dataset upon publication, extensive appendices with prompts/features/rubrics/configurations, detailed system prompts and expert evaluation protocols

Practical insights for post-training: finding that preferences don't uniformly reward dimensions and vary by domain directly informs RLHF/DPO design; careful prompt categorization captures workflow-level variation beyond subject domains

Sophisticated engagement with domain: recognizes that spreadsheet usage is workflow-dependent, establishes 6-category taxonomy capturing real usage patterns, provides realistic professional finance evaluation
weaknesses: Key finding under-investigated: formula sophistication features (lookups, conditionals, embedded constants) show no statistical significance despite being central to spreadsheet quality. The paper identifies this paradox but doesn't explore root causes—are voters unable to assess quality? Do models use similar patterns? Does feature extraction fail? This deserves deeper investigation given implications for preference-based training

Expert-crowd misalignment inadequately analyzed: only 42.3% agreement with arena (56.4% decisive)—barely above chance—yet analyzed as secondary. For professional domains with clear standards, this finding deserves front-and-center discussion. What drives disagreement? Are crowds systematically underweighting correctness? Limited to finance domain with modest sample (52 battles, 134 evaluations) and low inter-rater reliability (α=0.27-0.51)

Feature-adjusted compression raises unresolved questions: dramatic Elo shifts when controlling for features (Claude: −217, Qwen3: +157) suggest preferences heavily confounded by surface features, but implications for true model quality and whether adjustment masks important differences are not explored

Statistical power concerns for domain-specific claims: ~120 battles per domain and ~36 per model/domain limits power for detecting domain effects. The dramatic Academic finding (Claude drops 8 ranks) is striking but based on limited data

Limited methodological novelty: Bradley-Terry modeling, feature-augmented regression, and failure taxonomy are established techniques from Chiang et al. (2024), Scale AI (2025), and Deng et al. (2025). Contribution is primarily application to new domain rather than methodological innovation

Insufficient problem-solution focus: paper identifies concerning patterns (formatting>correctness in preferences, expert-crowd misalignment, formula sophistication irrelevance) but proposes limited solutions. How should RLHF be conducted if formatting drives preference more than quality? Should professional domains use different evaluation paradigms?

Architecture choice constraints: single end-to-end JSON generation may not reflect iterative human or production spreadsheet building. While acknowledged, impact on generalizability of findings is not explored

Model coverage and analysis: 16 models heavily skewed toward frontier closed systems. Limited open model coverage. Finding that Claude shows distinctive failure signatures (high Integrity/Numerical, low Spec Non-compliance) is interesting but underdeveloped—no systematic analysis of model-family differences

strengths: Addresses important understudied domain: spreadsheet generation affects ~500M users but receives minimal research attention compared to code generation

Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation combining arena votes (4,357), programmatic feature analysis (29 features), data-driven failure taxonomy, and domain expert evaluation—more thorough than typical single-metric evaluations
Excellent experimental rigor: proper blinding, Benjamini-Hochberg corrections, feature-augmented Bradley-Terry model that cleanly decomposes preference sources, and fully-crossed expert design

Rich nuanced findings revealing domain-specificity: feature effects vary dramatically across categories (p < 10⁻⁶⁸), model families exhibit distinct failure signatures (e.g., Claude loses on correctness while others lose on presentation), and features like finance_color_convention are significant only within domain
Feature adjustment reveals substantial confounding: leaderboard compression from 918 Elo to 550 points shows formatting/structure features bias raw rankings, validating need for decomposition
High-quality reporting: extensive appendices with complete methodology, SheetSpec specification, evaluator instructions, example spreadsheets, and detailed failure taxonomy definitions
Practical contribution: live platform, dataset release (1,033 prompts + 4,357 votes), and code release promise to support future research
weaknesses: Critical validity concern: expert-arena agreement is only 56.0% (63.6% for decisive comparisons), barely above chance, with low inter-rater reliability (Krippendorff's α = 0.28-0.45). This raises fundamental questions about whether crowd votes reflect genuine quality versus preference bias (formatting, verbosity). Paper acknowledges but doesn't investigate causes or implications

No training/improvement experiments: paper claims findings 'have implications for post-training' (p.3) but provides no RLHF or finetuning experiments validating this. Without demonstrating that insights improve models, practical impact is limited to infrastructure

Limited methodological novelty: Bradley-Terry models (Bradley & Terry 1952), feature-augmented BT adapts Scale AI (2025), arena evaluation from Chiang et al. (2024), failure taxonomy methodology from Deng et al. (2025). Primarily applies existing techniques to new domain rather than developing novel methods

Formula sophistication features show no significant effects (lookup p=0.73, conditionals p=0.28, constants p=0.55) despite being central to generation tasks. This surprising null result lacks investigation—unclear whether it reflects crowdworker inability to evaluate correctness, prompts not emphasizing it, or formatting overwhelming evaluation

Expert evaluation severely limited in scope and reliability: only 25 finance battles (vs. 500+ prompts), low inter-rater reliability undermines confidence, overall expert rating 2.86/5 with only 16.1% circulation-worthy. Missing analysis of whether gap reflects models' fundamental incapability or evaluation miscalibration

Voter identity unspecified: paper doesn't disclose arena voter demographics or expertise (crowdworkers vs. researchers vs. domain specialists), yet this substantially affects interpretation. Chiang et al. (2024) specified 'community voters,' but this paper doesn't

Feature interpretation conflates correlation with quality: text density (+1.56), fills (+1.15), numeric content (+1.02) are strongest predictors. Unclear if this captures genuine quality or mirrors 'length bias' seen in dialogue evaluation (Hu et al. 2025)—needs analysis of actual user utility

Presentation issues: paper attempts to cover too much (rankings, features, failures, expert eval), making some sections rushed. Critical finding (expert-crowd misalignment 56%) mentioned in passing. Domain-specific feature variation (§5.2.2) deserves more prominence—this is a key insight

strengths: Addresses practical, understudied task (spreadsheet generation) with 500M real-world users
Multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining arena votes, programmatic features (29 extracted), data-driven failure taxonomy, and expert domain evaluation is thorough
Feature-augmented Bradley-Terry analysis reveals interpretable model differences and shows feature effects vary substantially across domains
Promises to release substantial dataset (4,357 votes, 1,033 prompts) and live arena
Generally well-written with clear motivation and good visual examples
weaknesses: Critical validity issue: only 56% agreement between crowd preferences and expert standards (barely above 50% chance); 66.4% in follow-up study barely improves this; low inter-expert reliability (α = 0.28–0.45) raises fundamental questions about what the arena measures

Limited methodological novelty—applies established techniques (Bradley-Terry, feature regression, LLM judges) to new domain without advancing methods; 78% validation accuracy for failure taxonomy is adequate but not strong

Key findings are incremental and somewhat expected: 'formatting matters more than formula sophistication' and 'preferences vary by domain' lack deep investigation of mechanisms; no causal analysis of why Claude models dominate despite apparent formatting weaknesses

Missing comparative evaluation against existing benchmarks (SpreadsheetBench, SheetCopilot, SheetRM mentioned but never evaluated); cannot assess whether arena captures different signal than programmatic evaluation
Seed prompts from 'expert contributors' with unclear institutional affiliation; k-NN prompt categorization error rate not reported; training data contamination not analyzed; generalization unclear
Arena design choices unjustified: no ablation on 4 battles per prompt, 16 model selection, or initialization scheme; no inter-rater agreement study for crowd votes themselves

Table 4 shows presentation deficiency has no correlation with win rate (r = -0.376, p = 0.15), contradicting Section 5.2's claim that formatting strongly predicts wins; feature collinearity and confounding not addressed

Limited model analysis depth: why do Claude models dominate? No investigation of architectural/training differences, emergent capabilities, or feature importance by model family; no ablations or error analysis
Practical value unclear: Impact Statement provides only vague recommendations; no guidance on whether to optimize for crowd or expert preferences; no validated interventions

strengths: Addresses important, understudied problem (spreadsheet generation with 500M users); first comprehensive evaluation framework for this domain
Comprehensive multi-method evaluation combining arena voting, feature decomposition, data-driven failure taxonomy, and expert rubric—triangulation approach is more robust than single signal

Domain-specific feature analysis is insightful: shows preference drivers vary substantially across categories (e.g., has_border: -0.87 in Creative vs. +0.57 in Finance), with implications for domain-adaptive training
Key finding that formula sophistication (conditionals, lookups) lacks significance (p>0.28) while formatting/text density drive preferences challenges assumptions and informs RLHF design

Excellent reproducibility: releases dataset (4,357 votes, 1,033 prompts), live arena, code, and detailed specifications (SheetSpec@2 schema, model configs, failure taxonomy validation) enabling community use
Data-driven failure taxonomy with semi-automated categorization pipeline (clustering → LLM judge → expert validation) is clever; Table 4's correlations link failure modes to arena performance

Honest limitations discussion: acknowledges expert-crowd misalignment (56%), low inter-rater reliability (α=0.28-0.45), feature-adjusted scores as decompositions not counterfactuals, computational costs—intellectual honesty strengthens trust
Well-organized presentation with clear motivation, logical structure, and extensive rigorous appendices (K-M) documenting methodology thoroughly
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Bradley-Terry model with feature covariates (Eq. 1) closely follows Scale AI (2025); primarily applies existing techniques to new domain rather than developing new methods

Expert-crowd misalignment (56% agreement, 63.6% decisive; expert α=0.28-0.45 inter-rater reliability) suggests crowd and expert preferences measure different constructs; follow-up study (66.4%) on only 25 battles leaves this central concern incompletely resolved

Causal interpretation issues with feature decomposition: 217-point Elo compression for Claude Opus after feature adjustment is striking but causality unclear—features could be proxies for underlying quality rather than true drivers; acknowledged as 'decompositions, not counterfactuals' but then used for ranking interpretation throughout §5.2 without sufficient caveats

Failure taxonomy validation thin: LLM judge validated on only 50 samples (1.1% of battles); 78% alignment acceptable but 22% unvalidated; Table 4 shows 'Numerical Computation' and 'Integrity' failures near-zero correlation with arena (r≈0.0±0.06), suggesting either poor capture or non-discriminative taxonomy

Statistical rigor concerns: 5 of 16 significant features lose significance under conservative Benjamini-Yekutieli correction; no pre-registered hypotheses; no formal tests comparing feature effects across domains; some findings fragile (e.g., pct_number_format p<0.001 overall but p=0.065 in Academic)

Limited expert evaluation scope: only 50 spreadsheets (0.6% of votes) from finance domain only; 5–8 min per review is brief; binary circulation question lacks nuance; no error analysis of systematic expert-crowd disagreement types

Prompt and voter characteristics underexplored: seed prompts authored by unnamed 'expert contributors' with unclear process; category imbalance (Professional Finance 25% vs Academic 5%); voter expertise/background not characterized; k-NN classification of new prompts could propagate biases

Single-pass JSON generation paradigm limits applicability; real professional workflows often involve refinement. Alternative structured representations might yield different preferences. Results may not generalize beyond this format

Missing comparative analysis: no comparison to alternative evaluation methods (programmatic checks, other rubrics, user studies); limited investigation of why formula sophistication doesn't matter (is it users don't value complexity, or models rarely generate correct complex formulas?); minimal analysis of model family performance across tasks

Feature engineering is hand-engineered (29 features); no exploration of learned representations, feature selection, or importance via permutation/Shapley; some features proxy for 'effort' which could introduce bias if used for model training
